lead: Kansas City, Kansas grew up where the Kansas and Missouri rivers meet. Old homes, combined sewers and spring storms make basement water its most common problem.
risk: basement flooding, sewer backups and storm damage
why: In July 1951, the Kansas River flooded Armourdale and Argentine, two of the city's riverside neighborhoods. Homes, packing plants and rail yards were swamped, and thousands of people lost their homes. Higher levees went up afterward, and the river has been held back since. But the city's older areas still have combined sewers that carry rain and sewage in the same pipes, and heavy storms overload them.

About 76% of Kansas City, Kansas homes were built before 1980, and many have block or stone basements. When a spring storm fills the sewers, water backs up through basement floor drains. Old clay laterals crack and let in roots. Hail and strong winds are common too, and winter cold snaps freeze pipes in outside walls and older homes with little insulation.

tips: Install a backwater valve on the basement floor drain.
Add sewer backup coverage to your policy; it is usually extra.
Have an old sewer lateral scoped and roots cleared.
Get the roof checked after any hail, even with no leak yet.
areas: Calls come from Strawberry Hill, Rosedale, Argentine, Armourdale, Quindaro, Piper, Fairfax and Welborn, plus Bonner Springs, Edwardsville and Kansas City, Missouri.

faq.q: Why does my Kansas City, Kansas basement flood when it rains hard?
faq.a: In older parts of the city, rain and sewage share the same pipes. A heavy storm can fill them, and water backs up through the lowest drain in your home. A backwater valve stops most backups. Sewer backup coverage is usually an add-on, so check your policy.
